en: At the spring-fed stream of Batkaktuu,
All the holy men gathered.
They dipped their hands into water
And performed their ablutions.
Men endowed with sacred power had come;
To this imperial Beijing
Twelve pairs of khans had come.
Aykojo from Mecca had said,
“For the handful of Muslims
I shall serve as imam.”
Thus he had come to lead the prayers.
Loudly they called the call to prayer,
And gathered together.
When they came to seek their khans,
Khans Muzburchak and Kokcho were absent.
Bokmurun, son of Kokotoy,
That warrior, his only son, was absent too.
When they sought the forty companions,
Your lion Alma the leopard was absent;
Precious Chubak the wolf was absent;
Syrgak, son of Khan Ulak, was absent.
The support on which they girded themselves was gone.
Among the forty champions,
With mighty Alma at their head,
Twelve wolves were absent!
When they entered this Beijing,
It had been a road cut by Khizr.
At that time, when the Muslims
Took a count of their people,
Their army had been forty-two san.
The people’s khans were absent;
Manas grieved and sobbed.
The reason for his sobbing—
All those precious ones were gone!
In Beijing, where he had waged his campaign,
Your warrior had lost Akkula to a bullet
And sent Almambet to a martyr’s death.
His wing had been broken;
He had lost Khan Chubak, his trusted support.
He had raided Beijing and taken much;
Yet all the champions,
Through neglect, Manas had consumed!
Khans Muzburchak and Kokcho had died;
All who encountered Beijing had died.
He was struck from the flank.
All the mighty men—
Your warrior had let China take them as gifts!
Those who came died, souls died;
They were slaughtered in Beijing.
Warrior, all who encountered it died.
“I have the strength,” he had said as he came,
Manas the leopard, thundering.
Demanding Beijing and then turning back,
Whom he had cherished as a gift—
Having lost the warrior, steadfast Syrgak,
Unable to cease grieving,
The noble khan raged;
Instead of dying, he became a blaze,
His wretched soul beyond restraint.
In the mud of the dark spring water,
With Aykojo as their imam,
While they were saying their prayers,
Argyn Khan’s Ajybai,
Who knew the tongues of seventy tribes,
A man of consummate skill,
When they bowed their heads in prayer,
Was standing guard at that time.
Argyn Khan’s son Ajybai
Gripped his spear and leaned upon it;
Your warrior fell into a light doze.
That Ajybai had fallen asleep,
Alooke’s Kongurbay,
Your crafty hero lying in wait,
Watched and noted carefully.
Then, his great boots jutting out,
His neck held high like a rooster’s,
With his painted pipe bearing a golden moon,
That fierce man, great as a hut,
His saddle flaps fluttering,
A coral stone big as a leather flask
Shook upon his head.
Jerking his golden reins,
Driving Algara forward,
With a face like oiled wheat,
Alooke’s Kongurbay,
His eyes like twilight mist,
When the fierce man looked from afar,
They had dipped their hands in water;
All the Muslims
Had fallen in rows upon the ground,
And were bending head down.
The fierce warrior, who knew the enemy’s ways,
Had seen them from afar.
Bright dawn had broken,
Light had fallen on the earth.
That the warrior was lying thus,
The wretched fierce man had understood.
The black-cheeked battle-axe
Alooke’s Kongurbay
Had hanging at his wrist.
With its point forged of steel,
Tempered in dragon’s venom
In sixty separate immersions,
Leaving none unharmed when thrust,
Letting none it met escape alive,
The painted spear in his hand
The fierce warrior gripped and swung round.
Algara beneath him—
The wind could not catch his trot.
Khan Manas had not raised his head from prostration;
Kongurbay did not cease riding forward.
While Manas remained bent over,
“The surface of his spine,” he said,
“The place beside his lung,” he said.
Alooke’s Kongurbay,
Sparing nothing, with both hands,
Thrust with exceptional force.
Then Manas the leopard,
While Kongurbay was thrusting,
Untroubled by the ringing blows,
Kongurbay’s spear
The warrior counted as nothing at all.
Courage and lionlike prowess
Had been bestowed upon the hero without measure.
“If the obligatory prayer is broken,
That will be worst of all,” he said.
Reaching his right hand back,
The warrior seized the spear.
Noble Manas, the precious lion,
When he jerked the spear,
The painted spear that was stabbing him
Shattered into eighty pieces.
Alooke’s Kongurbay
Turned back, urging his horse on,
And fled in a clattering rush.
Then Argyn Khan’s Ajybai
Burst out from the flank.
The accomplished lord Ajybai
Struck Kartkurong with his whip,
And reached him sooner than an arrow.
As soon as he reached the fierce man,
He thrust into his side as he passed.
Kongurbay was wounded;
Then that swine was in a bad way.
When he groaned, “Oh!” from his mouth
Blood came gushing again and again,
And Kongurbay’s strength ebbed away.
That bastard’s Black Horse,
His Black Horse had
Wings upon its sides.
Whenever he met trouble anywhere,
It was always like this—
The horse would flee, as was its habit.
The forty or so lords beside him
Did not come near to aid their comrade.
Cloud gathered in the sky,
And the formidable fierce man, that noble lion,
With life hanging between death and survival,
Escaped in full sight of them.
His breast could not contain his many cares.
“God has plainly struck me!” he said.
Ajybai’s tears streamed in ten directions.
“While standing guard upon the rise,
I relaxed and fell asleep,” he said.
“I have earned the warrior’s displeasure,
I have disgraced myself,” he said.
“Will these Muslims standing here
Not learn of my doglike conduct?
‘You have done it twice, not once!’ they will say.
Will they not ride me like a black donkey?”
Not a single soul knew
How the Chinese man had stabbed him;
No one had found out.
By sleeping, he had let Manas be stabbed,
Yet Ajybai had no cause for regret.
Then Argyn Khan’s Ajybai,
Before your generous lord,
Dismounted in agitation,
The great lead-rope tied with rounded knots
He wound about his neck,
With both hands upon his breast,
He gave Manas his greeting;
Ah, warrior, Ajybai came pleading:
'Here stands a city with its sovereign;
“Ah, warrior, here I am—take my head!
I offer before you
A horse such as Kartkurong here;
Since my eyes were overcome,
Ah, warrior, here is blood to pour by the flaskful!”
Then Manas stirred his great frame,
Your warrior heartened, speaking boldly:
“Ajybai, do not shrink from this hard task;
Pull the spear out of my waist.
Ajybai, let no one see you!
Over the spear within my waist,
Let the great host not grieve;
Let the Muslims not grow sorrowful,
And those left living among the dead,
Warrior, let them not lose heart!”
Ajybai hurried up to help;
The belt around his waist
Clung to the warrior’s spear.
Told to pull straight, he pulled it slack,
And when he twisted the spear,
The steel point gave a crack
And broke off within the warrior’s waist.
Then his many sorrows overflowed his breast;
Bereft of his fierce wolves,
Then his tears streamed in ten directions:
“The crow that flies with croaking cries
Will gouge the flanks of noble men,” he thought.
“The martyrs fallen on campaign
Will turn to the shit of beasts,” he thought.
Searching through the hills, he saw
The brim of the black felt cap—
Syrgak, the leopard’s champion.
The warrior had gone straight to Mecca.
The warrior had gone straight to Mecca.
Then, fallen in the flower of his days,
Ah, warrior, struck down in his youth!
The giant Kutan and giant Mangkush,
The Lama and enormous Joloy—
He had killed all four alike,
Offering them in sacrifice,
Cutting off their heads and tying them on,
Taking them as gifts;
When Syrgak wreaked havoc,
Of ninety myriads of Black Chinese,
When yesterday he broke apart their ranks,
Beginning with their giant Kutan,
When he slaughtered ninety giants,
Never turning back, he dealt your Chinese people
A crushing blow that broke their backbone.
He missed the foe he should have met
And met the one he should not meet;
Whirling his spear and breaking ranks,
He encountered Kojojash,
And the warrior fell a martyr to a shot.
Having first wrought slaughter,
My Syrgak died a martyr—
Ah, warrior, at twenty-one!
Noble Syrgak, the leopard,
Fallen in the flower of his days,
With the holy Quran for his pillow,
Ah, warrior, his head toward the qibla.
Where Syrgak’s soul departed,
Its back broken upon the ridge,
His horse Kokchebich died beside him.
In the ravine of It-Kyya,
Muzburchak and Khan Kokcho died.
At the farthest corner of the mountains,
The warrior Bokmurun had died as well.
Then thirteen souls he found upon the plain;
When he saw the mighty fallen,
Your mighty Manas, the leopard,
There, in the forest’s green recess,
